newsitem.title: CROATIA: U.N. praises Croat concessions to rebel Serbs.
newsitem.headline: U.N. praises Croat concessions to rebel Serbs.

text.p: The United Nations on Monday welcomed a human and minority rights package Croatia has offered to Serbs in the rebel enclave of Eastern Slavonia, saying the deal was better than anticipated.

"We are very, very pleased with the document... I think (Serbs) will be very pleased by it and I think it basically gives much more than they had imagined," Jacques Klein, head of the U.N. transitional mission in Eastern Slavonia (UNTAES), told reporters after meeting Croatian President Franjo Tudjman.
The memorandum was first presented by a visiting Croatian delegation on Saturday.
It offered the Serbs the right to vote where they lived before the 1991 war, exemption from military service for those with "objections of conscience" and a seat in the National Parliament.
Government and U.N. sources confirmed on Monday that some changes to the memorandum, taking into account the Serbs' objections, had since been made.
The military exemption for "a cooling off period of two years" and two seats in the parliament instead of one were now being offered, they said.
The Croatian constitution offers Western-style human and minority rights to Serbs but diplomats say Zagreb has often lacked political will to respect them despite verbal pledges to do so.
"It's one of the best packages I've seen," Klein said, adding he would soon forward it to the U.N. Security Council "for consideration".
"This should aid markedly the progress of holding the elections (there) on March 16, moving the process of peaceful integration and ending the UNTAES mandate by early summer," Klein said.

The mandate in Eastern Slavonia should end on July 15 after minority Serbs take part in a countrywide local election, due in March, for the first time since they rebelled against Croatia's independence from federal Yugoslavia in 1991.
About half of some 120,000 Serbs currently living in Eastern Slavonia are refugees from other rebel enclaves recaptured by Zagreb troops in two blitz attacks across U.N. ceasefire lines in 1995.
The offensives sent up to 200,000 Serbs fleeing for safety to Serb-held Bosnia and Yugoslavia. Most of them are still there, fearing reprisals despite a general amnesty Zagreb declared last year.
Croatia has been severely criticised by the United Nations for harassing the mostly elderly Serbs who remained in their former enclaves and for hindering the return of other refugees.
